query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor amount of aluminum (e.g., 2–5 at%) to a CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy will promote the in situ formation of a continuous, lubricious alumina-based spinel oxide layer during sliding, thereby maintaining a low coefficient of friction and low wear rate from room temperature up to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy with a nanocrystalline microstructure
generation.intervention: Incorporate a controlled alloying addition of aluminum into the CoCrFeNi matrix
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests performed in air under comparable loads for both room temperature and elevated temperatures up to 800 °C
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a nanocrystalline, adherent alumina-based spinel oxide tribofilm at the sliding interface
generation.mechanism: At higher temperatures, the Al addition facilitates rapid oxidation to form a stable, protective oxide scale that reduces metal-to-metal contact, friction, and wear. At room temperature, the modified microstructure preserves mechanical integrity while still allowing formation of a thin oxide layer that aids lubrication.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Al-doped CoCrFeNi alloy will exhibit a consistently lower coefficient of friction and reduced wear rate relative to the undoped alloy, across the temperature range from ambient to 800 °C.
generation.baseline: Tribological performance of the original CoCrFeNi alloy without aluminum addition
generation.boundary: Tests conducted in air with sliding contact under loads similar to previous studies, with temperatures ranging from room temperature to 800 °C
generation.uncertainty: The optimal Al concentration for balancing oxidation protection with mechanical properties is uncertain; the exact quantitative improvements in friction and wear are also subject to further experimental calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one with the baseline CoCrFeNi composition and one with an added 2–5 at% Al. Conduct sliding wear tests in air at room temperature, then incrementally increase the temperature up to 800 °C while maintaining similar load and sliding speed. Analyze the tribological performance (coefficient of friction and wear rate) and use surface analysis (e.g., XRD, SEM, TEM) to detect the formation of alumina-based oxide scales.
measurements: Coefficient of friction (COF) at room temperature and 800 °C
Wear rate (mm³/N·m) across the temperature range
Phase identification of surface oxides via XRD
Microstructural observation of the tribofilm via SEM/TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-doped alloy does not show a statistically significant reduction in COF and wear rate compared to the baseline CoCrFeNi alloy at elevated temperatures, or if no continuous protective alumina-based oxide layer is observed on the worn surfaces, then the hypothesis will be rejected.

Question: How can a nanocrystalline refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film with superior mechanical and tribological properties be synthesized using a cost-effective single target, and what are the effects of annealing on its adhesion and wear performance?. System: Equimolar CuMoTaWV refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film deposited on silicon and 304 stainless-steel substrates. Processing: DC-magnetron sputtering using a single target prepared by partial spark plasma sintering (SPS) of equimolar elemental powders (Cu, Mo, Ta, W, V) at 1000 °C under 40 MPa pressure; film deposition at 500 °C substrate temperature for 120 min in Ar atmosphere (1.16 × 10⁻³ mPa, 150 W power); post-deposition annealing at 300 °C for adhesion improvement. Test conditions: Nanoindentation at 3 mN load; nanopillar compression (440 nm diameter, 3 mN max force); tribological wear tests at room temperature (RT) and 300 °C with 1 N load and 0.1 m/s sliding speed against E52100 alloy steel counterballs. Findings: The as-deposited film exhibited a nanocrystalline body-centered cubic (BCC) solid solution with an average grain size of 18 nm and a thickness of ~900 nm.; Nanoindentation measurement

Question: How does the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy change under reciprocating wear conditions at elevated temperatures, and what are the underlying mechanisms?. System: AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEA). Processing: Inert gas atomisation using argon followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 1050 °C for 10 min under 50 MPa compaction pressure, with passive cooling at 150 K/min until 300 °C.
